bib.title: Follow-the-Regularised-Leader and Mirror Descent (Bandit Algorithms, Chapter 28)
bib.venue: book chapter, Bandit Algorithms (Cambridge University Press)

question: How can follow-the-regularised-leader and mirror descent give efficient, low-regret algorithms for online linear optimisation and adversarial linear bandits?
contributions: Define mirror descent and FTRL, show when they coincide and when they differ
Exponential weights and Exp3 recovered as special cases
Efficient FTRL for adversarial linear bandits on the unit ball with regret O(sqrt(dn log n)), a sqrt(d) improvement over continuous exponential weights

limits: Chapter is theory only: no experiments, no empirical comparison, no wall-clock or compute figures.
Note 6: no characterisation of which potential to use; no known way to find it, especially for bandits.
Note 9: bounds for non-oblivious adversaries do not transfer to the bandit setting; the non-oblivious regret needs empirical-process tools and gives O(sqrt n) only if the variance is O(n).
Unit-ball algorithm needs the horizon n to tune eta (Note 7: use doubling or decreasing learning rates, where FTRL is preferred over mirror descent).
Mirror descent and FTRL are identical only for Legendre F with domain inside A and a constant eta; otherwise they differ.
Dimension dependence for general action sets is not well understood (Note 10).
practices: Use FTRL (sum of past loss estimates, then argmin of regularised loss) instead of unregularised follow-the-leader, which has linear regret on adversarial sequences (Sec 28.1, Ex 28.4, Note 11).

Match the potential to the geometry: Euclidean for the ball, unnormalised negentropy for the simplex (gives exponential weights/Exp3), since the wrong potential costs a factor of sqrt(d/log d) (Ex 28.9).
Implement mirror descent in two steps: an unconstrained update in the dual space via (grad F)^-1(grad F(a_t) - eta y_t), then a Bregman projection onto A (Sec 28.1.1).
With bandit feedback, replace the loss vector by an unbiased importance-weighted estimate and play a random action whose mean is the iterate (Algorithm 16, Sec 28.3).
On the unit ball, shrink the action set to radius r<1 to keep the estimator variance bounded near the boundary (Sec 28.4).
When the horizon is unknown use a decreasing learning-rate schedule; FTRL is usually preferred over mirror descent here (Note 7, Ex 28.11-28.13).
Online gradient descent is mirror descent with a quadratic potential on linearised losses (Example 28.1, Note 12).

terms.definition: a_{t+1} = argmin_{a in A} (eta <a,y_t> + D_F(a,a_t)), with a_1 = argmin F
a_{t+1} = argmin_{a in A} (eta sum_{s<=t} <a,y_s> + F(a)): the action that performed best in hindsight on the regularised loss
the convex (usually Legendre) function F that defines the algorithm
the function grad F, which maps primal actions to the dual space
full-information version of the adversarial linear bandit, where the learner observes the whole loss vector y_t
a_{t+1} = argmin sum_s <a,y_s> with no regularisation; unstable on adversarial losses
mirror descent with F=1/2||a||^2 on compact A: a_{t+1} = Pi(a_t - eta y_t)
simplex with unnormalised negentropy gives a_{t+1,i} proportional to exp(-eta sum_s y_si)
the extra regret from observing <A_t,y_t> instead of y_t; sqrt(d log n) on the unit ball
